The revision petitioner herein challenges the conviction and sentence against him under Section 16(1)
(c) (d) read with Section 10(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (P.F.A Act) and Rule 12 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules in S.T 7026/1997 of the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Chalakudy.

entities.label: STATUTE

entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: He is the licensee of the grocery shop being run in the building No.22/231 of the Chalakudy Municipality.

The said prosecution was brought against the revision petitioner by the Food Inspector of the Chalakudy Municipality, on the allegation that when the Food Inspector visited the shop of the revision petitioner at about 11.30 a.m on 15.11.1997 for collecting sample of Bengal-gram (channa) for analysis, he was obstructed and threatened by the revision petitioner, and when the Food Inspector demanded 750 gms of Bengal-gram, the revision petitioner declined the request.
According to the Food Inspector, he had also prepared the Form VI notice to be given to the accused.
2. The accused appeared before the learned Magistrate and pleaded not guilty when the substance of the accusation was read over and explained to him.
The Food Inspector examined himself and also his Office Peon, and proved Exts.P1 to P6 documents.
The accused denied the incriminating circumstances when examined under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
He did not adduce any evidence in defence.
3. On an appreciation of the evidence, the trial court found the accused guilty.
On conviction, he was sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for three months by judgment dated 19.11.2001.
Aggrieved by the judgment of conviction, the accused approached the Court of session, Thrissur with Crl.A 614/2001.
In appeal, the learned III Additional Sessions Jude, (Adhoc-I), Thrissur confirmed the conviction and sentence and accordingly dismissed the appeal.
4. On hearing both sides and on a perusal of the materials, I find that the prosecution case is suspicious, and that there is no legal evidence to sustain the conviction.
PW1 is the Food Inspector who filed the complaint, and PW2 is his office peon.
It is pertinent to note that PW2 does not in any manner support the Food Inspector.
He did not state anything in evidence regarding the alleged obstruction or intimidation made by the accused.
This witness was not declared hostile or cross-examined by the learned Public Prosecutor .

2 5.

According to the Food Inspector, he visited the shop of the accused at about 11.30 a.m on 15.11.1997 and just when he disclosed his identity and stated that he had come to collect sample for analysis, he was threatened and obstructed by the accused.
Ext. P3 said to be the Form VI notice prepared by the Food Inspector.
It is not known how and why he prepared a Form VI notice there, if he were really intimidated or obstructed at the very beginning itself.

There was no occasion for the Food Inspector to prepare or give a Form VI notice, if the accused actually threatened and obstructed him just when he disclosed his identity and stated the object of his visit.
Thus, the Ext.P3 Form VI notice creates some doubt regarding the truth of the prosecution case.
The complaint shows that the Food Inspector demanded 750gms of Bengal-gram from the total quantity of 35 kgs kept there for sale.
It is not known how he could assess the total quantity kept there for sale.
In evidence, his case is that he demanded sample from the total quantity of 55 kgs of Bengal gram kept there for sale.
Thus, he is not consistent as regards the total quantity.
If he were really obstructed by the licensee, it requires explanation how he could correctly assess the total quantity of Bengal gram kept there for sale.

6. The evidence of the office peon will not in any manner prove the prosecution case, and it will rather improbabilise the case of the Food Inspector that he was threatened and obstructed by the licensee.
PW2 has no such case that the Food Inspector was obstructed or threatened by the licensee.
I find that there is no legal and satisfactory evidence proving the allegations beyond reasonable doubt.
In such a circumstance, the accused will have to be acquitted.
In the result, this petition is allowed.

The revision petitioner is found not guilty of the offence alleged against him under Section 16(1) (c) (d) read with Section 10(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (P.F.A Act) and Rule 12 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and he is acquitted of the said offence in revision.
